extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer professionals, university IP managers, and practitioners implementing or advising on TRIPs obligations
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and substantive provisions from the WTO TRIPs agreement relevant to protection, enforcement, exceptions, and administration of intellectual property rights, intended to guide national implementation and technology-transfer practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark nonuse and abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that abandonment requires nonuse of at least three years without a valid reason for the nonuse; certain excuses for nonuse outside the trademark owner’s control (e.g., import restrictions and other government requirements) are to be recognized as valid reasons; third-party use under the control of the owner of the mark shall inure to the benefit of the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This changed U.S. law extending the abandonment period from two to three years; demonstrates that legitimate external impediments to use must be accepted before invoking abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of encumbrances on trademark use
rubrics_metrics.description: Encumbrances on the use of a trademark (such as requirements that its use must be linked with some other mark) are barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member territories must not impose conditions that force marks to be used only in conjunction with others, protecting independent use rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on compulsory licensing and free assignment restriction for trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Although member countries may impose conditions on the terms under which trademarks may be licensed, compulsory licensing of trademarks is banned as are prohibitions on the right of a trademark owner to assign a trademark without transfer of the business to which the mark belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territories may regulate licensing terms to prevent anti-competitive clauses, but may not force compulsory trademark licenses nor block assignment separate from the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against misleading geographical indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Member territories are required to make provision for interested parties to prevent use of a designation that falsely indicates the geographical origin of goods if this is done in a way that misleads the public as to the geographical origin of the good and to prevent or cancel registration of a trademark if this would have a similar effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are more specific protections for wines and spirits (multilateral notification/registration system) and ongoing negotiations to increase GI protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design protection requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Member territories must provide protection for new and original independently created industrial designs for a period of at least ten years. No need to protect a design dictated essentially by technical or functional considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection may be by industrial design law or copyright and must provide protection against articles embodying a copy or substantial copy of the protected design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent nondiscrimination (availability and enjoyment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be available and enjoyable without discrimination as to the place of invention, the field of technology, and whether the product is imported or produced locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes changes such as 35 U.S.C. 104 amendments to avoid discrimination against inventions made abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible exclusions from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The only types of inventions countries can exclude from patentability are (a) those whose exploitation would prejudice public order or morality; (b) those involving diagnostic, therapeutic, or surgical methods for the treatment of humans or animals; (c) plants and animals; or (d) essentially biological processes for the production of plants or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries that exclude new plants must provide some alternative means of protection for such plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 30 limited exceptions to patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries may allow limited exceptions (e.g., experimental-use or personal-use rights) provided such rights do not unreasonably conflict with normal exploitation of the patent and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the patent owner, taking account of legitimate interests of third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions must be narrow and balanced against the patentee’s interests; Article 30 sets the test of 'not unreasonably conflict' and 'not unreasonably prejudice'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for compulsory licenses and official licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory licenses or other 'official licenses' are only to be permitted after consideration of the individual situation; any such license shall be nonexclusive and assignable only with the business that enjoys its use; except in national emergency cases, requester must have made efforts to obtain a voluntary license on reasonable commercial terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional specified conditions: predominantly for domestic market supply; termination if circumstances cease; adequate compensation; independent review of compensation; cross-licensing only where the later patent is an important technical advance of considerable economic significance relative to the dominant patent and cross-license entitlements apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing and public health (Doha-related guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In health crises (e.g., HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria), member states may: apply customary rules of interpretation (read provisions in light of objectives), grant compulsory licenses and determine grounds, determine what constitutes a national emergency or extreme urgency (public health crises can qualify), and establish their own exhaustion regime (parallel imports) subject to MFN and national treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doha ministerial declaration clarified flexibility for public health; subsequent waiver (2003) and amendment (2005) permit use of compulsory licensing for export to countries lacking manufacturing capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimum duration of a patent is to be twenty years from its filing date (may be calculated from date of original application in continuing cases). Transitional provisions ensure patents still in effect when a country becomes bound have this term applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This led to U.S. change from 17 years from grant to 20 years from filing; transitional calculations apply for continuing applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of burden of proof in process-patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement for reversal of the burden of proof in patent infringement trials involving patents granted for processes: there shall be a presumption that a product that could have been made by the process was made by the patented process if either (a) the product itself is new or (b) there is a substantial likelihood that the product was made by the patented process and reasonable attempts by the patentee have been unable to find out exactly what process was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges difficulty of proving process infringement in jurisdictions lacking discovery similar to U.S. practice; reversal helps enforcement of process patents abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum rights conferred by a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is for a product the patentee must have the exclusive right to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling that product or importing the product for any of these purposes; where the patent is for a process, the patentee must have the exclusive right to prevent third parties from using, offering for sale, selling or importing at least the product obtained directly by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines baseline scope of exclusionary rights for product and process patents under TRIPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for topographies of integrated circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Member territories must provide protection for the design of integrated circuits as set out in relevant treaty articles and additionally to grant protection for semiconductor chip design for a period of at least ten years from filing or first commercial exploitation, whichever first occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision includes a limited defense for 'innocent' infringers and applies most provisions on compulsory licensing of patents to IC designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for undisclosed information (trade secrets and regulatory data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Member territories are required to provide protection for 'undisclosed information' that is secret (not generally known or readily accessible), has commercial value because it is secret, and has been subject to reasonable steps by its owner to keep it secret; such information must be protected against use by others without consent if contrary to honest commercial practices, including use by third parties who knew or were grossly negligent in not knowing information was obtained dishonestly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member territories must also take adequate steps to protect confidentiality of data about new chemical entities submitted to government authorities for marketing approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of anticompetitive contractual license terms
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPs recognizes that territories may legitimately seek to prevent inclusion of anticompetitive terms in IP licenses (exclusive grant backs, prohibitions on challenges to validity, coercive package licensing are examples). Territories whose nationals are affected have a right to be consulted on application of such laws to their nationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows member states to police license clauses for competition concerns while providing consultation rights to affected foreign parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement procedures: availability and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Member states must ensure enforcement procedures are available to permit effective action against IP rights covered by TRIPs, including expeditious remedies to prevent infringement and act as a deterrent; enforcement procedures should be fair and equitable; decisions on merits should 'preferably be in writing and reasoned' and based only on evidence on which the parties were offered an opportunity to be heard; there should be an opportunity for judicial review of administrative decisions and at least of legal aspects of initial judicial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets procedural fairness standards for civil/administrative remedies, provisional measures, border measures, and criminal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness in acquisition/registration and inter partes review
rubrics_metrics.description: Member states shall ensure procedures for grant or registration permit granting or registration within a reasonable period to avoid unwarranted curtailment of protection; procedures used in granting/registering rights or in administrative revocation must comply with fairness and equity and administrative refusal or revocation must be subject to review by judicial or quasi-judicial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to prevent unduly burdensome, costly, or delayed registration and to provide review avenues for administrative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 43 disclosure/production of evidence in proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 43 requires member states to provide means whereby, under appropriate circumstances, a judicial tribunal can order production of evidence (useful where discovery is otherwise limited). Production of such evidence is subject to steps to protect confidential information; if a party fails to produce ordered information, courts must be able to decide the proceeding against the offending party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balances need for evidence production with confidentiality protections; adverse consequences for non-production are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum remedies available for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 44 requires member countries to provide for injunctions to order a party to desist from infringement and prevent entry into channels of commerce of infringing goods. Article 45 requires damages 'adequate to compensate for the injury' and allows award of attorney fees to IP holders who prove infringement. Article 46 allows judicial authorities to order disposal or destruction of infringing goods and materials and implements primarily used to create infringing goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies must be adequate to compensate and deter; courts have broad remedial powers including destruction of goods and fee-shifting in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and limits of provisional remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement to improve availability of provisional remedies: judicial authorities must have authority to act promptly to prevent infringement and/or preserve evidence and, in appropriate circumstances, to act even without giving the alleged infringer the right to be heard; the unheard party must be given an early opportunity to challenge any remedy and remedies may be subject to indemnity for wrongfully enjoined parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows ex parte provisional relief with safeguards (early challenge, indemnity) to balance speed and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special requirements for border measures (customs enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members (unless in a customs union that makes border measures impracticable) must set up procedures enabling trademark and copyright owners to lodge applications to prevent importation of counterfeit trademark goods or pirated copyright goods. To invoke this, right holder must establish a prima facie case and provide a sufficiently detailed description of the goods; a security may be required; customs shall hold goods for ten working days after notice to give right holder opportunity to commence proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs action is subject to evidentiary showing and protections to prevent abuse and protect importers (security/deposit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal procedures and penalties for large-scale counterfeiting/piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Member states are required to provide for criminal procedures and penalties at least in cases of trademark counterfeiting and copyright piracy on a commercial scale; available remedies must include imprisonment and/or monetary fines 'sufficient to provide a deterrent' consistent with penalties for crimes of corresponding gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures that egregious commercial-scale IP crimes can be met with criminal sanctions of deterrent severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: WTO dispute settlement timelines and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispute resolution is confined to disputes between member territories about compliance with WTO obligations. Prior to formal proceedings there is a 60-day consultation period. Panels of experts (normally 3) are set up; panel must make decision on merits within six months. Parties typically have two hearings and may submit comments on drafts; final report goes to General Council and becomes ruling unless rejected by consensus within sixty days. Either party can appeal to the Appellate Body (3 of 7 members) which must give opinion within 90 days; General Council accepts or rejects within 30 days. Remedies/sanctions confined to international trade (e.g., authorized retaliatory tariffs) and confined to relevant sector where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes timeliness compared to earlier GATT practice and the multistage process leading to trade-sanction authorization where compliance/compensation fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aid and technology transfer obligations for developed countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles 66 and 67 call for developed countries to encourage technology transfer to least-developed territories and for developed countries to assist developing and least-developed countries in implementing TRIPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames TRIPs implementation as including capacity-building and assistance obligations toward less-developed members; least-developed countries have extended transition periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation/transitional provisions for developing and least-developed countries
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPs came into effect January 1, 1996 with phased implementation: developing nations given until Jan 1, 2000 (and five years to expand patent protection to all areas of technology); least-developed countries given ten years for many aspects except general principles; national laws (e.g., U.S. Uruguay Round Amendments Act) were amended to implement TRIPs (patent term change, use of foreign inventions evidence, copyright restorations, trademark nonuse period extended to three years, GI rules for wines/spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation timetables differ by development status; specific national legislative changes illustrate compliance steps and timing.
